# oxframe 0.5.0

Text of this version of the documentation. Code samples are the fenced blocks from the pages.

Welcome to oxframe

  oxframe lets you make animations by writing code. You describe what happens, step by step, and
  oxframe turns it into a video — with a live editor to scrub through it and fine-tune the timing.

 Here is a whole animation: a square slides to the right and becomes a circle.

#[oxframe::scene]
async fn intro(view: View)

  If that reads like a recipe —  add a square, then move it and round its corners at the same time  — you already understand the main idea. The rest of these docs teach you the details, one small step
  at a time.

 How to read these docs

     Start here  gets oxframe running. If you just want to look around first, open
    the
     playground : it runs in your browser, nothing to install.

     Guide  is ten short lessons. Each one adds a single idea and has a live preview you
    can play with. Read them in order — none of them assumes more than the lessons before it.

     Going further  is the reference: every node, effect, editor feature and command.

    Under the hood  explains how oxframe works inside, for the curious.

 What you need to know

  The basics of Rust are enough:  let , functions, and calling methods. You do not need
  to know
   async  — lesson 1 explains the only part of it you will use. No graphics experience required.

  Ready?  Install oxframe , or jump straight to
   lesson 1  in the browser.

Working with AI agents

  Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex or Cursor can write oxframe scenes for you. Every new
  project comes with instructions that teach them how — and a way for them to see what they made.

 What  oxframe init  adds

        AGENTS.md

        The project's rules for any agent: how scenes work, which commands to run, what never to do
        (non-deterministic code, editing  meta.json  by hand) and fixes for the most common
        compile errors.

        CLAUDE.md
       One line,  @AGENTS.md , so Claude Code reads the same file.

        .claude/skills/oxframe/

        A skill with a step-by-step workflow ( SKILL.md ) and an API cheat sheet ( reference.md ). Agents that support skills load it whenever you ask for a change to a scene.

 The files are plain Markdown. Read them, edit them, add your own project conventions.

 Letting the agent see its work

  Animation is visual, so compiling is not enough to know a change is right. The instructions tell
  the agent to look at the picture after every change:

oxframe check                 # storyboard.png + report.json; exit 1 on errors
# open out/check/storyboard.png and out/check/report.json, fix, run again
oxframe inspect --at 2.5      # scene tree at that time, when a frame looks wrong

  The storyboard is a grid of frames with the time under each cell. The report names the rule, the
  node and the source line.  oxframe snapshot  is still there for one full-size still.
  Nothing keeps running —  oxframe dev  is for you, not for the agent.

 A good way to work together

   Keep  oxframe dev  open in your browser.

    Ask the agent for a change in plain words:  "after the title, slide three cards in from the left, one after another" .

    The agent edits the code and checks it with  oxframe check ; your preview reloads by
    itself.

    Fine-tune timing yourself with markers and sliders. The agent is told to keep your
     meta.json  values, so your adjustments survive its next edit.

 Keeping the files up to date
 After upgrading oxframe, refresh the instructions:

oxframe agents          # refreshes the generated files
oxframe agents --force  # also replaces files you made your own

  Generated files carry an  oxframe-agents  marker comment. To keep your own version of a file,
  delete that comment — files without it are left alone. Projects created with an older CLI can get the
  files the same way.

 Connecting an MCP client

   oxframe mcp  speaks MCP over stdin and stdout. Point Claude Code, or any other client,
  at that command with the project directory as its working directory. The tools are
   check ,  storyboard ,  render_frame ,  inspect ,
   list_components ,  docs_search  and  render .
   docs_search  looks through the docs of the CLI's own version.

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "oxframe":
  }
}

  Every command also takes  --json  and then prints a single JSON object on stdout. A
  compile error includes the compiler text and a  hints  array for the mistakes agents
  make most often (a forgotten  .await , a builder never passed to  add , a
  theme token used as a number, and the rest).

 For tools that read the web

  Each docs version has a plain-text index and a full dump, generated from the pages when the site
  is built. The current version is   /llms.txt   and
    /llms-full.txt  . A pinned version is
   /docs/<series>/llms.txt  (for example
    /docs/0.1/llms.txt  ). The current series redirects to
  the unversioned files, so a link written for today's version keeps working after that series is
  archived.

Camera

  A camera zooms, pans and turns the view of everything added to it. Show a whole diagram, move in
  on one detail, follow something as it travels — while titles stay put.

 World and screen

  Add a  Camera  to the view and build the world inside it. Everything you add to the camera
  is seen through it; everything you add to the view itself stays on screen, which is where titles, captions
  and labels belong.

let cam = view.add(Camera::new());
let diagram = cam.add(Group::new());      // the world: seen through the camera
diagram.add(Rect::new().width(360.0).height(160.0));
view.add(Txt::new().text("Title").h2().to_edge(Edge::Top)); // on screen

 Moving the camera

  A camera has four signals, animated like any other property:  x  and
   y  are the point it looks at,  zoom  is how close it is (2 = twice as big),
  and  rotation  turns the view (in degrees, clockwise).

cam.fit(diagram, 120.0, 0.0).await;   // all of it in the frame, 120 px to spare
cam.center_on(api, 1.0).await;         // bring one node to the middle
cam.zoom().to(2.5, 1.0).await;         // move in
cam.rotation().to(15.0, 1.0).await;    // tilt
cam.reset(1.2).await;                  // back to x = y = 0, zoom 1, no rotation

   fit  measures the node when it is called, so a layout that has grown is framed at its
  current size. A duration of  0.0  jumps there at once — handy for the first frame. To
  move and zoom together, run both in  all :

  all((cam.center_on(api, 1.2), cam.zoom().to(1.6, 1.2))).await;

 Following a node

  Bind the camera's position to a node and it follows it every frame. The next animation of the
  camera's  x  or  y  releases it.

let (px, py) = (packet.x(), packet.y());
cam.x().bind(move || px.get());
cam.y().bind(move || py.get());
packet.x().to(900.0, 2.0).await;       // the camera rides along
cam.fit(diagram, 120.0, 1.4).await;    // and lets go here

 Sharp at any zoom

  Nothing is stretched: every frame is drawn again at its final scale. Text and outlines stay crisp
  at ×10, and blurs, shadows and glows grow with the zoom instead of turning to mush — on the GPU
  and the CPU renderer alike.

 Checking

    oxframe check   does not report nodes inside a camera as out
  of frame: when you zoom in on a detail, the rest of the world is supposed to be outside. Text overlap
  and contrast are still checked, and nodes added to the view are checked as usual.

CLI reference

  Everything the  oxframe  command can do. You will use  dev  most of the time;
  the rest are for creating, checking and exporting.

 The everyday loop

oxframe init my-video     # once: create a project
cd my-video
oxframe dev               # edit code, watch the preview update
oxframe render            # when you are happy: out/my-video.mp4

 Commands

  Every command accepts  --json . It then prints one JSON object on stdout ( ok ,  exit , and on failure  error ,  diagnostics  and
   hints ) and keeps the log on stderr.

  oxframe init <name>

  Creates a folder with a ready-to-run project:  Cargo.toml  (SDK version pinned),
   src/main.rs  with one scene, its  meta.json ,  oxframe.toml ,
   .gitignore  and instructions for AI coding agents (see
   Working with AI agents ).

       --sdk-path <dir>   Use a local  oxframe-sdk  checkout instead of crates.io (also
         OXFRAME_SDK_PATH ).

  oxframe dev

  Builds the project, opens the editor in your browser and rebuilds every time you save. If the code
  does not compile, the error shows over the preview and the last good build keeps playing.

       --port <n>   Editor port (default 3000).
       --open  /  --no-open   Open the browser, or don't (overrides  oxframe.toml ).
       --release   Optimized build: slower to compile, faster to play heavy scenes.
       --cpu   Render the preview on the CPU — useful on machines without a working GPU.

  oxframe snapshot --at <seconds>

  Renders single frames as PNG without ffmpeg — handy to check a moment in the animation, to put a
  still in a README, or for an AI agent to look at its own work.

oxframe snapshot --at 1.5                       # out/snapshots/ -1.50.png
oxframe snapshot --at 0 --at 2 --at 4           # three frames
oxframe snapshot --at 1 --out cover.png         # exactly this file
oxframe snapshot --at 0.5 --scene outro         # time from the start of a scene

  Each written file is printed on its own line ( path frame=N t=T ), so scripts can pick
  them up. Default size is 960×540; change it with  --size 1920x1080 .

  oxframe render

  Builds in release mode and renders a video. See  Rendering video  for examples.

       --out <path>   Output file or folder (default  out/<project>.mp4 ).
       --format <f>    mp4 ,  webm ,  prores  or  png ; by default
        taken from the  --out  extension.
       --scene <name>   Only this scene.
       --range a..b   Only this time range, in seconds; either side can be left out ( 2.. ).
       --size WxH   Output size, e.g.  3840x2160 .
       --aspect <shape>    16:9 ,  9:16 ,  1:1 , or  all .
         all  writes one file per format declared with
         Project::aspects .
       --cpu   Use the CPU renderer, e.g. in CI without a GPU.
       --no-audio   Leave the soundtrack out.

  oxframe check

  Compiles the project ( cargo check ), validates every  meta.json , compares
  the versions of the CLI, SDK and editor, and then looks at the picture. It writes
   out/check/storyboard.png  (a grid of frames at markers and at equal intervals, with
  the time and marker name under each cell) and  out/check/report.json .

  Each issue has a rule, a severity ( error  or  warning ), a time range, the
  node name, the source  file:line  and a hint:

     out_of_frame  — a node stays outside the frame (or inside the frame but outside the safe
    area, which is a warning).

    text_overlap  — two text blocks cover each other.

     text_overflow  — text is wider than its  max_width  or its layout parent.

    low_contrast  — text against its backdrop is below WCAG 4.5:1.

     too_fast  — a long line flashes too briefly to read (error), or a large move is shorter
    than 0.15s (warning).

     dead_time  — nothing on screen changes for several seconds and the project has no soundtrack
    (warning).

  Errors make the command exit 1; warnings do not. A project that declares
   Project::aspects  is checked in every format; the other storyboards are
   storyboard-9x16.png  and  storyboard-1x1.png .  --frames  also
  writes each cell at full size under  out/check/frames/ . The check renders only the
  frames it needs, on the CPU, at a reduced size, so a 30 second scene finishes in a few seconds.

  Name a node with  .name("title")  so the report is readable. Without a name it is
  labeled by the line that called  add .

  oxframe inspect --at <seconds>

  Prints the scene tree at that time as JSON: kind, name, source location, scene bounds, opacity,
  text and draw order.  --scene outro  measures the time from the start of that scene.

  oxframe agents

  Writes or refreshes  AGENTS.md ,  CLAUDE.md  and
   .claude/skills/oxframe/  — run it after upgrading oxframe. Files you edited yourself
  are left alone unless you pass  --force .

  oxframe upgrade

  Moves the project to the SDK version your CLI is made for: updates the  oxframe  pin in
   Cargo.toml  (keeping your formatting), runs  cargo update  and refreshes the
  agent files. If the project already uses a newer SDK, it tells you to update the CLI instead.

  oxframe mcp

  An MCP server on stdin and stdout, for Claude Code and other clients. Started in a project, it
  serves  check ,  storyboard ,  render_frame ,
   inspect ,
   list_components ,  docs_search  and  render . Messages are
  newline-delimited JSON-RPC; a  Content-Length  frame is accepted too. Nothing but the protocol
  is written to stdout.

 Updating

cargo install oxframe-cli --force   # a new CLI
oxframe upgrade                     # then in each project

  Projects pin the SDK version, so a release never changes an existing project on its own. Once a
  day the CLI checks crates.io in the background and mentions a newer version; set
   OXFRAME_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1  to turn that off.

 oxframe.toml
 Project settings for the CLI. Every key is optional.

[dev]
port = 3000
open = true        # open the browser on "oxframe dev"
profile = "dev"    # or "release"

[render]
ffmpeg = "/opt/ffmpeg/bin/ffmpeg"   # default: ffmpeg from PATH

[theme]
name = "dark"         # dark, light, midnight, paper, vivid
accent = "#68abdf"    # one brand color; other colors stay readable

[check]
interval = 1.0        # seconds between storyboard frames
safe_inset = 48       # px; 0 turns the safe-area warning off
min_contrast = 4.5
min_motion = 0.15
max_still = 3.0
chars_per_second = 20
min_chars = 24
cell_width = 320

 Exit codes

      0  Success.
      1  Your code does not compile, the scene fails, or  oxframe check  found an error.
      2  Environment: no ffmpeg, port in use, cannot write a file.
      3  Version mismatch between the CLI, SDK and editor.

 Add  -v  to any command for detailed logs.

 Security

  The editor server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, checks the  Origin  of every WebSocket connection
  and requires a one-time token. The CLI runs nothing but cargo and your own project.

The editor

  A tour of the editor. It is the same app under  oxframe dev  on your machine and in the playground
  on this site.

 The four areas

   Viewport

    The current frame. Scroll to zoom around the cursor, hold  Alt  (or the middle button) and
    drag to pan, double-click to fit. Click a node to select it.

   Timeline

    Play, pause and scrub. Shows scene boundaries, markers and the soundtrack's waveform. Drag a
    marker to retime everything that waits for it.

   Inspector

    The node tree, the live values of the selected node's signals, sliders for  tune!
    values and the list of named eases.

   Curve editor

    Opens when you click an ease. Drag the two handles or pick a preset; a dot previews the motion.

 When code does not compile

  The compiler's message appears over the viewport with the file and line. The last build that
  worked keeps playing, so you never lose your place. Fix the code and save — the error goes away by
  itself.

 Shortcuts

       Space   Play / pause
       ←   →   Previous / next frame
       Shift + ←   →   Jump 10 frames
       Home   End   Start / end
       M   Move the selected marker to the playhead
       Esc   Close dialogs, dismiss errors

 Small conveniences

    The frame, zoom and selection are kept in the URL — a reload or rebuild returns you to the same
    spot.

   Several browser tabs can be connected to one  oxframe dev  at the same time.
   In the playground,  Share  puts the whole source into the link.

Effects

  Gradients, dashes, shadows, blur, blend modes and clipping. Every effect is a signal, so it
  animates like any other property —  .to() ,  .ease()  and
   .bind()
  all work.

 Paint

Rect::new()
    .fill_gradient(Gradient::linear((-100.0, 0.0), (100.0, 0.0)).stops([color!("#e13238"), color!("#f5c242")]))
    .stroke(Color::WHITE).line_width(4.0)
    .dash(vec![12.0, 8.0])          // animate dash_offset for marching ants
    .line_cap(LineCap::Butt)

  Gradients are in the node's own coordinates (origin at its center).  Gradient::radial(center, radius)  works the same way. Two gradients with the same number of stops interpolate.

 Layers

  A node is drawn into its own layer when its effect must apply to the node and its children as a
  whole: group opacity (overlaps do not get darker), blend modes, blur and shadows. Plain shapes
  skip the layer and stay fast.

Group::new().opacity(0.5)                         // group opacity
Circle::new().clip(true).child(...)              // children clipped to the circle
Circle::new().blend(BlendMode::Multiply)         // Multiply, Screen, Overlay, …
Txt::new().blur(12.0)                            // Gaussian blur (σ, node units)
Rect::new().shadow(Color::BLACK.with_alpha(0.6), 16.0, (0.0, 12.0))
Circle::new().glow(color!("#68abdf"), 20.0)      // shadow without offset

 Order and pivot

Rect::new().z_index(-1.0)            // drawn below its siblings
Rect::new().anchor((-1.0, -1.0))     // (x, y) is the top-left corner and the rotation pivot

  Blur and shadows are rasterized by the same code on both renderers (tiny-skia), so CPU and GPU
  output match; only the area a layer can touch is processed.

Install and first project
 Five minutes from nothing to an editor with your own animation in it.

   Want to skip installing?  Everything in the guide also works in the
   playground . Come back here when you want to render videos on your
  machine.

 1. Install the tools
 You need Rust and, to make videos, ffmpeg.

# Rust (skip if you have it)
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

# ffmpeg
sudo apt install ffmpeg        # Linux
brew install ffmpeg            # macOS
winget install Gyan.FFmpeg     # Windows

# the oxframe command
cargo install oxframe-cli

 2. Create a project

oxframe init hello
cd hello
oxframe dev --open

  The first build takes a minute or two — Rust compiles the engine once. Then your browser opens the
  editor: the animation in the middle, the timeline at the bottom. Press  Space  to play.

 3. Change something

  Open  src/main.rs , find  color!("#68abdf")  and change it to
   color!("#2ecc71") . Save. About a second later the editor shows the new color — and
  stays on the same frame. That loop, edit → save → look, is how you will work.

 4. Make a video
  oxframe render        # writes out/hello.mp4

 What is in the project

       src/main.rs   Your scene. Everything you write goes here.
       src/intro.meta.json   Timing values you adjust in the editor (lesson 7). Commit it.
       oxframe.toml   Settings for  oxframe dev  and  render .
       assets/   Images and audio.
       AGENTS.md ,  .claude/   Instructions for AI coding assistants (see  Working with AI agents ).

  Next,  lesson 1  walks through that first scene line by line.

Components

  An explainer is a handful of blocks. Each one takes its color and type from the theme, places
  itself, and answers  enter ,  next  and  exit .

 Title card

let title = view.add(TitleCard::new("Binary search").subtitle("O(log n)"));
title.enter().await;
title.next().await;
title.exit().await;

  enter  fades the card and the title in.  next  reveals the subtitle.

 Chapter marker

let chapter = view.add(ChapterMarker::new("1  Search"));
chapter.enter().await;

 A label pinned to the top safe area, including on a vertical frame.

 Bullet list

let steps = view.add(BulletList::new(["Take the middle", "Compare", "Drop half"]));
steps.enter().await;
for _ in 0..steps.len()

  enter  shows the stack. Each  next  reveals one row.

 Code explainer

let code = view.add(
    CodeExplainer::new("lo + (hi - lo) / 2").step(1, 1, "the middle"),
);
code.enter().await;
code.next().await;

   enter  shows the source. Each  next  focuses the next line range (1-based, inclusive)
  and sets the caption. A light theme uses a light code theme.

 Flow diagram

let flow = view.add(FlowDiagram::new().edge("Client", "API").edge("API", "DB"));
flow.enter().await;
for _ in 0..flow.len()

  You name the links. The diagram lays the nodes out in layers, left to right.
   .down()  stacks the layers.  next  highlights the next node.

 Callout

let card = view.add(Rect::new().size(280.0).fill(Surface));
let call = view.add(Callout::new(card).text("the middle"));
call.enter().await;
call.next().await;

  The caption sits above the target.  enter  draws the arrow,  next  shows the words.

 Lower third

let lower = view.add(LowerThird::new("Ada").role("walks the half"));
lower.enter().await;
lower.next().await;

 Pinned to the bottom safe area.  next  reveals the role.

 End card

let end = view.add(EndCard::new("That's the search").note("Repeat from the top"));
end.enter().await;
end.next().await;
end.exit().await;

 Same rhythm as a title card. The note waits for  next .

  The gallery example  components  is a full explainer in under 40 lines.
   Project::aspects  makes  oxframe check  look at 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1.

9. Drawing and morphing
 Draw an outline as if with a pen, then turn one shape into another.

 Drawing an outline on

  Every outline has two properties,  start  and  end , that say which part of
  it is drawn — as a fraction of its length.  .end(0.0)  hides it; animating
   end
  to 1 draws it on. Animating
   start  to 1 afterwards erases it from the beginning.

 Paths and morphing

  A  Path  is any shape you can describe with lines and curves — usually written in SVG
  path syntax ( "M0 -150 L44 -46 ..." ), which every vector tool can export. Animating
   data  to another path morphs between them. oxframe lines up the two outlines first, so a
  star turns into a heart without twisting.

  shape.data().to(heart, 1.2).await;

     Morph back to the star at the end.
     Animate  start  to 1 to erase the outline.

      start / end  control how much of an outline is drawn.
      Path  +  data().to(other_path)  morphs shapes.

4. Easing
 Why some animations feel natural and others feel robotic — and how to choose.

  All three balls travel the same distance in the same time. The difference is  easing : how the speed changes along the way.

    LINEAR  moves at a constant speed. It looks mechanical.

    The  default  starts slowly, speeds up, and settles in. Real objects move like this,
    which is why it is the default.

     OUT_BACK  overshoots a little and comes back — playful, good for things popping in.

  ball.x().to(500.0, 1.5).ease(presets::OUT_BACK).await;

   presets  has the common curves ( IN_OUT_CUBIC ,  OUT_EXPO ,
   IN_OUT_SINE , …). There are also bouncy ones:  .ease(oxframe::bounce_out)
  and  .ease(oxframe::elastic_out) .

     Try  presets::IN_OUT_EXPO  on the middle ball.
     Give the last ball  oxframe::bounce_out .

       .ease(...)  after  .to(...)  picks the curve; the default is a smooth in-and-out.

     In lesson 7 you will edit curves visually instead of picking presets.

7. Tweak timing in the editor

  Some things are easier to adjust by eye than by number. oxframe lets you do that without touching
  code.

  When an animation should start "on the beat" or a size "looks right", guessing numbers and
  recompiling is slow. These three helpers move the decision into the editor:

       wait_until("go").await   A  marker  on the timeline. Drag it, and everything after it moves.
       tune!("size", 160.0)   A number with a  slider  in the inspector; 160 is the starting value.
       .ease(ease!("move"))   An easing curve you shape in the  curve editor .

 Where the values live

  The first time your scene runs, oxframe writes these names and their starting values into a file
  next to your code,
   src/<scene>.meta.json . From then on the file wins: the editor changes the file,
  the code only provides defaults. Commit the file — it is part of your animation.

{
  "eases":  ,
  "markers":  ,
  "tunables":  ,
  "version": 1
}

      Open the lesson in the playground. Drag the  go  marker to the right on the timeline.

     Move the  size  slider in the inspector.
     Click the  move  ease in the inspector and bend the curve.

     Markers, tunables and named eases are values you adjust in the editor.
     They are saved in  meta.json ; the code only sets defaults.

6. Groups and layout
 Put shapes inside other shapes, and let a layout arrange them for you.

 Children

  So far everything was added to the  view . You can also add shapes to other shapes:
   sun.add(...) . A child's position is measured from its parent, and it moves, rotates
  and fades along with it. Rotate the sun, and the planet orbits; rotate the planet, and its moon
  orbits the planet.

  Group  is a shape that draws nothing — a container for others.

 Layout

  Placing ten cards by hand is tedious. A  Layout  places its children in a row (or
   .column() ), with  .gap()  between them and  .padding()  around.
  It works like flexbox on the web: children can  .grow(1.0)  to fill space, the row can
   .wrap(true) , and
   .grid(3)  makes a three-column grid.

  Layout settings are animatable like everything else. Animate the gap and the cards slide apart;
  remove a card and the others close the gap.

     Add  .width(500.0)  to the row and  .grow(1.0)  to one card.
     Add a second moon to the planet.

      parent.add(child)  — children follow their parent.
      Layout  arranges children: row, column, wrap, grid, grow.

1. Your first animation

  You will add a circle to the screen and move it. That is most of what animation code ever does.

 A scene is a function

  An animation in oxframe is called a  scene , and a scene is just a function marked
  with
   #[oxframe::scene] . It receives the  view  — the canvas you draw on.

  The word  async  is there because the function runs  over time : it can stop,
  let a few frames pass, and continue. You do not need to know more about  async  than that.

 Adding a shape
  let ball = view.add(Circle::new().size(160.0).x(-400.0).fill(color!("#68abdf")));

   Circle::new()  starts describing a circle; each  .something(...)  sets how
  it looks at the start — 160 pixels wide, 400 pixels left of the center, light blue.
   view.add(...)
  puts it on screen and gives you back  ball , a handle you use to animate it later.

 The center of the screen is (0, 0). Positive x goes right, positive y goes  down .

 Animating it
  ball.x().to(400.0, 1.0).await;

  Read it as:  take the ball's x, move it to 400 over 1 second, and wait until that is done.

     ball.x()  is the ball's horizontal position. Without an argument it gives you the property;
    with one (like in the builder) it sets the starting value.

     .to(400.0, 1.0)  creates the animation: target value, then duration in seconds.

     .await  plays it and waits. The next line only runs once the ball has arrived.

  So the scene plays its lines from top to bottom, and every  .await  takes time. That is the
  whole model.

      Open this lesson in the playground (link under the preview) and change  1.0  to
       3.0 .

     Add  ball.fill().to(color!("#e13238"), 1.0).await;  before the last line.

      What happens if you remove the  .await  at the end of a line? (The compiler will tell
      you.)

     A scene is an  async fn  with  #[oxframe::scene] .
      view.add(Shape::new()...)  adds a shape and returns a handle.
      handle.property().to(value, seconds).await  animates and waits.

10. Randomness and background tasks

  Lots of things happening on their own, while the main story continues — and still the same video
  every time.

 Random, but repeatable

   random()  gives a number between 0 and 1,  random_range(a, b)  one between
  a and b. They look random, but they come from the project's  seed  ( Project::new(..).seed(7) ), so every run — in the editor, in the final render, on another computer — produces exactly the
  same confetti. Change the seed for a different, again repeatable, result.

  This is a rule worth knowing: oxframe renders the same frames every time. That is why scenes must
  not use the clock or other sources of real randomness.

 Background tasks

   {'spawn(async move  )'}  starts an animation that runs on its own, while the
  scene continues with the next line. Each confetti piece is spawned, falls, and removes itself.
   spawn
  returns a handle you can
   .await  later to wait for the task — here the title waits for the confetti to finish.

     Change the seed.
     Make the pieces fall slower: change  2.0  to  4.0 .

       random()  and  random_range()  are seeded: same video every time.

      spawn  runs animations in the background.

 You made it

  That is the whole core of oxframe. From here, browse  all nodes  and
   effects , open the
   quicksort showcase
  to see everything working together, or read
   how oxframe works  inside.

3. Shapes, colors, transforms

  More shapes, outlines, and the properties every shape shares: rotation, scale, color.

 The shapes

   Rect ,  Circle ,  Polygon ,  Star  and
   Line
  are all made the same way:  Shape::new() , then settings.  Rect  has
   .radius()
  for rounded corners,
   Polygon  has  .sides() ,  Line  takes a list of points and can have
  arrows.

 One name, two uses
 This is the pattern you will use everywhere, so it is worth a second look:

   Before adding:  .size(140.0)   sets  the starting size.

    After adding:  .size()   gives you  the size, ready to animate with
     .to(...) .

 Things every shape has

     x ,  y  — position;  rotation  — degrees, clockwise;
     scale
    — a pair, so you can stretch ( Vec2::new(1.4, 0.7) ).

     fill  — the inside color;  stroke  and  line_width  — the outline.

    opacity  — 0 is invisible, 1 is solid.

  Colors are written  color!("#e13238")  (checked when you compile — a typo is an error, not
  a surprise). When a color animates, it blends through perceptually even shades instead of going muddy
  in the middle.

     Give the hexagon an outline:  .stroke(Color::WHITE).line_width(8.0) .
     Animate  star.points()  from 5 to 9.

      All shapes are built the same way and share position, rotation, scale, fill, stroke, opacity.

      .name(value)  sets before adding;  .name()  animates after.

 Themes

  A scene with no colors and no font sizes of its own already looks finished. Nodes take those from
  the project theme:  .fill(Accent) ,  .padding(Md) ,
   .radius(Lg) ,
   Txt::new().display() . Text with no fill uses the theme's text color.

Project::new("explainer").theme(Theme::dark().accent(color!("#68abdf")))

let title = view.add(Txt::new().text("Binary search").display());
let note = view.add(Txt::new().text("O(log n)").caption().fill(Muted));
title.fade_in().await;

  Built-in themes:  dark  (the default),  light ,  midnight ,
   paper  and  vivid .  .accent(color)  rebuilds the palette from
  one brand color and keeps text at a 4.5:1 contrast. The same override can live in
   oxframe.toml  without a recompile:

[theme]
name = "midnight"
accent = "#68abdf"

   fade_in()  and a duration of  Fast ,  Normal  or
   Slow
  use the theme's motion. One  .theme(...)  line changes every token in the video.

 Relative position and frame shape

  Place a node against another node or the safe area instead of counting pixels. The position is
  worked out again every frame, so it follows a neighbor that moves or changes size.  pct(80)  is 80% of the frame width.

let title = view.add(Txt::new().text("Binary search").h1().to_edge(Edge::Top));
let card = view.add(Rect::new().width(pct(80)).height(300.0).fill(Surface));
let label = view.add(Txt::new().text("mid").caption().next_to(card, Side::Bottom));

   align_to(other, Edge::Top)  shares an edge.
   center_in(other)  shares a center.
   to_edge  stops at the safe area: a portrait frame leaves room for a vertical video's
  status bar and buttons.  view.is_portrait()  and
   view.safe_area()  are there when a layout really does have to branch.

  Declare every shape the video should exist in.  oxframe check  looks at each of them,
  and  oxframe render --aspect 9:16  (or
   --aspect all ) exports them.

  Project::new("explainer").aspects([Aspect::Landscape, Aspect::Portrait, Aspect::Square])

 Every shape and all its settings are listed in  All nodes .

8. Signals

  Make one thing follow another automatically — a line that always connects two dots, a label that
  always shows a value.

 Every property is a signal

   a.x()  — what you have been animating — is a  signal : a value that can
  change over time. Besides  .to(...) , signals have  .get()  (read now),
   .set(v)
  (change now) and
   .bind(...) :

  label.x().bind(move || (ax.get() + bx.get()) / 2.0);

  This says:  the label's x is always halfway between the two dots.  Whenever a dot moves, the
  label follows by itself. In the preview only the two dots are animated; the line, the label and its
  text are all bound.

 About  move  and the extra lines

  The formula runs later, every time something changes, so it needs its own copies of the signals it
  reads — that is what  let (ax, bx) = (a.x(), b.x());  before it and  move  in
  front of it are for. Copying a signal is cheap: both copies point to the same value.

  Bound values are computed lazily — only when something needs them for drawing — so binding costs
  almost nothing.

     Bind  b.fill()  so the blue dot turns red when it gets close to the red one.
     Bind the label's  font_size  to the distance.

      Properties are signals:  get ,  set ,  to ,
       bind .

      bind(move || ...)  keeps a value up to date with a formula.

5. Text
 Titles, typewriter effects, mixed styles and code.

 Txt

   Txt::new().text("Hello").font_size(96.0).weight(800.0)  is a text shape. Two fonts are
  built in: Inter (default) and JetBrains Mono ( .family(MONO) ). Both include Cyrillic.
  Because the fonts ship with oxframe, your text looks exactly the same on every computer.

 Text animates too

     title.text().to("Hello, text", 1.0)  types the new text like a typewriter.

     .end()  from 0 to 1 reveals the text letter by letter (you will see  end  again
    for shapes in lesson 9).

     title.morph_to("New title", 1.0)  slides letters that both texts share into place and
    fades the rest.

 Mixed styles and code
  Txt::new().rich([span("Mix "), span("bold").bold(), span(" and "), span("color").color(color!("#f5c242"))])

   Code  shows source code with syntax highlighting, and can dim everything except the
  lines you are talking about:  Code::new().code(src).focus(3, 4) . The
   quicksort showcase  uses it heavily.

   code.code().to(next, 1.0)  does not type the new source. Tokens that stay slide to
  their new places, deleted ones fade, and new ones appear.
   insert(line, col, text, seconds) ,
   remove(((line, col), (line, col)), seconds)
  and  replace  edit one spot; lines are counted from 1 and columns from 0.
   .flash()  on that tween lights the inserted text for a moment. A focus on lines that
  move rides with them. The  code steps  example writes
  a function this way.

     Replace the typewriter with  title.morph_to("Hello, world", 1.0).await;
     Make the code bigger with  .font_size(48.0) .

       Txt  for text,  .rich([span(...)])  for mixed styles,  Code  for
      highlighted code.

      Animate  text  (typewriter),  end  (reveal) or call
       morph_to .

2. In order, or all at once

  In lesson 1 things happened one after another. Now you will make several things move at the same
  time.

 One after another

  Two lines, each ending in  .await : the second one starts when the first is finished.

a.x().to(500.0, 0.8).await;
b.x().to(500.0, 0.8).await;

 At the same time:  all

  To play animations together, put them in  all((...))  — note the double parentheses, it
  takes a group of animations — and await that once. It finishes when the  longest  one does.

  all((c.x().to(500.0, 0.8), d.x().to(500.0, 1.6))).await;

 Pauses and waves

   wait_for(0.3).await  simply waits.  stagger(0.1, &wave, |c| ...)  runs the same
  animation on every item of a list, each one starting 0.1 s after the previous — that is the ripple at
  the end of the preview.

  stagger(0.1, &wave, |c| c.y().to(200.0, 0.4)).await;

  For a list of the same animation that should all start at once,  all  takes it
  directly:
   all(wave.iter().map(|c| c.y().to(200.0, 0.4))) .

 Ready-made entrances

  Every shape has a few common moves built in. They take their length and easing from the theme, so
  a whole video stays consistent;  .duration(seconds)  changes one of them.

  title.fade_in().await;
badge.pop_in().await;              // grows from nothing with a small overshoot
card.slide_in(Side::Left).await;   // slides in from the left while fading in
outline.draw_on().await;           // the outline is drawn like with a pen
title.fade_out().duration(0.3).await;

     Wrap the two red squares in  all((...))  so they move together.
     Change the delay in  stagger  to  0.3 .
     Replace the wave's animation with  |c| c.pop_in() .

     Lines with  .await  run in order.
      all((a, b, c)).await  runs them together and waits for all.

       wait_for(seconds)  pauses;  stagger(delay, &list, |x| ...)  ripples through
      a list.

       fade_in ,  pop_in ,  slide_in ,  draw_on  are ready-made
      entrances.

How oxframe works

  You don't need any of this to make animations. Read it if you are curious why scrubbing is
  instant, why renders are reproducible, or how the playground runs Rust in your browser.

 A scene is a coroutine

   #[oxframe::scene]  turns your  async fn  into a future. oxframe polls it
  with a small single-threaded executor:  one poll is one frame . Each awaited
  animation updates its signals and returns "pending" until its time is up, so the code after it
  runs on the right frame.

  Time is virtual: each task keeps its own clock, advanced by exactly one frame per poll. A
   .to(x, 1.0)  that ends between two frames hands the remaining fraction to the next animation,
  so a long chain of steps never drifts from where the timeline says it should be.

 Everything is deterministic

  There is no wall clock and no thread pool in the scene code. Randomness comes from a ChaCha8
  generator seeded by  Project::seed , and every  spawn ed task runs in a
  fixed order. The same code and the same  meta.json  produce the same frames — on your laptop,
  in CI and in the browser.

  That is what makes seeking possible: to show frame 900, oxframe replays the scene from its start
  without drawing anything, which takes milliseconds, and then draws only the frame you asked for.

 Signals

  Every property — position, color, text — is a  Signal . A signal is either a value or a
  function of other signals ( .bind(…) ). Derived signals are lazy: they recompute only
  when read and only if something they depend on changed. Cycles are detected and reported instead
  of hanging.

 From nodes to pixels

    After each frame, the node tree is laid out (flexbox and grid via taffy) and flattened into a
     display list : fills, strokes, images and layers.

    A renderer draws the list.  vello  does it on the GPU through wgpu;
     tiny-skia  on the CPU. Layers with blur, shadow or glow are rasterized only within
    their bounds.

    For video, frames stream to  ffmpeg  through a pipe while the next ones are being drawn.

  Both renderers are checked against the same reference images: the average color difference must
  stay below ΔE 1 in OKLab, which is below what the eye can see.

 The editor and the engine

  Your project compiles into an ordinary binary.  oxframe dev  runs it as a preview
  server; the editor in your browser talks to it over a WebSocket with a small JSON protocol ( seek ,  play ,  set marker …) plus binary frames. When you save, the CLI rebuilds and
  restarts the binary, and the editor reconnects to the same frame.

  Edits to markers, eases and tunables go the other way: the editor sends them, the engine writes
   meta.json  and re-runs the scene — no compilation needed.

 The playground

  The playground sends your code to a compile service that builds it to WebAssembly in a sandbox
  (results are cached by the hash of the source and SDK version). The same engine then runs inside a
  Web Worker in your page. With WebGPU it renders on your GPU through vello into an
   OffscreenCanvas ; without it, it falls back to the CPU renderer. The editor speaks the
  same protocol to the worker as it does to  oxframe dev , so they behave the same.

 Where the code lives

       oxframe-sdk   The Rust crates: core (executor, signals, easing), 2d (nodes, layout), text, render,
        export, preview, protocol.
       oxframe-cli   The  oxframe  command and the embedded editor build.
       oxframe-web   The editor UI, this site, the playground and the compile service.

All nodes

  A reference of every node and its properties. If you followed the guide, you already know the
  pattern; this page is for looking things up.

  Builders set initial values;  view.add(builder)  (or  node.add  for
  children) returns a
   Copy  handle whose methods of the same names return signals.

     Node  Builder  Signals

       Rect    .width .height .size .radius    width height radius
       Circle    .size .start_angle .end_angle .pie    size start_angle end_angle  — arcs, pie slices
       Polygon    .sides .size    sides size  — sides animate
       Star    .points .size .inner    points size inner
       Path    .data(BezPath) .svg("M0 0 …")    data  — morphs
       Line    .points .smooth .closed .start_arrow .end_arrow    points arrow_size
       Txt    .text .rich([span(..)]) .font_size .weight .family .italic .align .max_width    text spans font_size weight ,  morph_to
       Code    .code .language .theme .focus(a, b) .dim    font_size focus dim ,  code().to  (a token diff),
         insert ,  remove ,  replace ,  focus_lines
       Img    .src(include_bytes!(..)) .file(path) .width .height    width height
       Svg    .src(include_bytes!(..)) .file(path) .width .height    width height ,  find("id") ,  paths()
       Layout    .row .column .wrap .grid(n) .gap .padding .align .justify .width .height    gap padding width height radius
       Grid    .width .height .spacing    width height spacing
       Group   —  —
        Camera     .zoom    zoom  (and  x y rotation ),  center_on fit reset

  Every node has  x y rotation scale opacity fill stroke line_width start end , the paint
  and compositing properties described in  Effects , and the flex
  item properties  grow shrink basis margin align_self .  start / end
  trim outlines — animate  end  from 0 to 1 to draw a shape on (on text it reveals glyph by
  glyph).

   Svg  reads a whole file and turns it into those nodes: groups stay groups, shapes
  become  Path s (so  data  still morphs), and embedded PNG or JPEG images
  become  Img .  find("id")  is the element with that id.
   paths()  is every contour in paint order. Filters, masks and clip paths are skipped
  with a warning. See the  logo example .

 Shapes and morphing

  Tweening  Path::data  between any two paths aligns them first (segment counts, start points,
  winding), so shapes morph without twisting.

 Layout

   Layout  is real flexbox (and CSS grid with  .grid(columns) ), computed by
  taffy. Children take
   .grow ,  .shrink ,  .basis ,  .margin  and
   .align_self ;
   LayoutAlign::Stretch  resizes rects, images and nested layouts. Layout properties are signals:
  animate the width or the gap and everything re-flows.

 Text

  Inter and JetBrains Mono are embedded (OFL), so text renders identically everywhere. Strings tween
  like a typewriter.

 Rich text, code and morphing

Txt::new().rich([span("Signals are "), span("lazy").bold().color(color!("#f5c242"))])
Code::new().language("rust").code(src).focus(3, 4)   // code.focus_lines(5, 5, 0.4).await moves it
code.code().to(next, 1.0).await                       // tokens slide; not a typewriter
code.insert(3, 0, "    let y = x * 2;\n", 0.6).flash().await
code.remove(((5, 0), (6, 0)), 0.5).await              // lines from 1, columns from 0
word.morph_to("frame", 1.0).await                    // shared letters travel, the others fade

  Highlighting covers Rust, JS/TS, Python, JSON, TOML and shell, with One Dark and One Light themes.

Rendering video

  When the animation looks right in the editor, one command turns it into a video file.

  oxframe render

  That's it: the project is built in release mode and every frame goes to  out/<project>.mp4 . You need  ffmpeg  installed for video formats; PNG frames
  work without it.

 Common recipes

oxframe render --out film.webm             # VP9 with transparency
oxframe render --format prores --out a.mov # ProRes 4444 with transparency, for video editors
oxframe render --format png --out frames/  # one PNG per frame
oxframe render --size 3840x2160            # 4K
oxframe render --scene outro               # just one scene
oxframe render --range 1..3                # seconds 1 to 3
oxframe render --cpu                       # no GPU available (CI, servers)

  Need just one still?  oxframe snapshot --at 2.5  writes a PNG of that moment — no ffmpeg,
  no full render.

 Sound
 Attach a soundtrack to the project:

Project::new("my-video")
    .audio("assets/voice.mp3")
    .scene(intro())

  The waveform appears on the editor's timeline; drag it to shift the sound against the picture. The
  offset is saved in  meta.json  and used by  oxframe render . Pass
   --no-audio  to leave it out.

 Transparent backgrounds

  Make the background transparent with  .background(Color::TRANSPARENT)  on the project
  and render to  webm ,  prores  or  png : those keep the alpha
  channel, so you can lay the animation over footage in a video editor. MP4 (H.264) has no
  transparency.

 GPU or CPU?

  By default frames are drawn on the GPU (vello) and fall back to the CPU (tiny-skia) when no GPU is
  available. Both produce the same picture: they pass the same reference-frame tests within a color
  difference of ΔE 1, which you cannot see. The CPU renderer is also byte-for-byte identical between
  runs, which is what you want in automated tests.

 In the browser

  The playground can export MP4 too (the  Export  button). It encodes with your browser's
  WebCodecs, so it works offline but is limited to what the browser supports — use the CLI for ProRes,
  4K or long videos.

Markers, eases, tunables

  The full story behind  lesson 7 : values that live outside
  your code so you can adjust them in the editor.

 The three kinds

wait_until("beat").await;                    // marker: a point on the timeline
x.to(300.0, 1.0).ease(ease!("slide")).await;   // named ease: a curve you can bend
let speed = tune!("speed", 1.4);               // tunable: a number with a slider

        Marker

         wait_until(name)  pauses the current task until the marker's time. The first time
        it runs, the marker is placed where the code reached it — so nothing changes until you drag it.

        Ease

         ease!(name)  is a cubic Bézier curve, like CSS  cubic-bezier() . It
        starts as a smooth in-out; edit it in the curve editor or pick a preset there.

        Tunable

         tune!(name, default)  returns a number. Use it for anything you want to dial in by
        eye: sizes, speeds, counts, delays.

 The meta file

  Each scene has a  src/<scene>.meta.json  next to its source. Code provides defaults;
  the file stores what you changed. Names missing from the file are added with their defaults the first
  time the scene runs.

{
  "eases":  ,
  "markers":  ,
  "tunables":  ,
  "version": 1
}

  Keys are sorted and unknown keys are preserved, so the file is safe to edit by hand and gives
  clean diffs. Commit it together with the code.

 Good to know

    Changing a value in the editor does  not  recompile — the preview updates instantly.

   Names are per scene. Two scenes can each have their own  "speed" .

    Renaming a marker in code creates a new one at its default position; the old entry stays in the
    file until you delete it.

    oxframe check  validates all meta files.

 A bigger example
 This chart uses a marker to sync the bars with a beat and named eases for their motion.
